Comments: No primary-source evidence was gathered in this run showing the Senegal revenue authority or treasury systematically collecting taxes/fees via a named national revenue-collection platform integrated with mobile money beyond sector examples (e.g., health premiums). revision_notes: Original 0/Unknown was mislabelled: a light check surfaced clear, official evidence of digital revenue collection, so this was moved to the full path. DGID's e-services platforms (E-services, Sen-ETAFI, Mon Espace Perso), officially relaunched 26 January 2026, allow online declaration and payment of income tax, VAT, corporate tax and other levies, and since November 2025 taxpayers can pay via the Orange MAX IT mobile money app ('Fay Sama Impôt'). Fetched and read DGID's own e-services page plus two independent press reports confirming the same official communiqué. Recalculated to 3 (Yes/comprehensive) given multiple tax types are payable digitally through official government-run channels.
revised_comments: Senegal's Direction générale des Impôts et des Domaines (DGID) enables digital payment of taxes and duties through several official channels. Since January 2026 the DGID's e-services platforms (E-services, Sen-ETAFI and Mon Espace Perso) allow taxpayers to declare and pay income tax, VAT, corporate tax and other duties online, and since November 2025 taxpayers have also been able to pay via the Orange MAX IT mobile money application. Payments are integrated directly with tax administration systems, with confirmation and receipts issued electronically.

Nineteen Senegalese institutions — including banks, mobile money issuers and microfinance institutions — are authorised PI-SPI participants, enabling business-facing payment flows on the interoperable rails.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: No credible, primary legal source confirming Senegal’s data breach notification obligations (mandatory vs discretionary) was retrieved within the current research set; targeted searches (Senegal data breach notification; CDP Sénégal breach reporting) were not completed to verifiable URLs in this run, so scored unknown.

revision_notes: A light check surfaced multiple, mutually conflicting sources, so this was moved to the full path rather than confirmed as a simple Unknown. Fetched and read a professional legal analysis (Mondaq/LPS Law) of the founding Data Protection Act (Law No. 2008-12, 2008), which explicitly states the law is silent on breach notification to the CDP or affected individuals; this is consistent with the full statutory text (via WIPO Lex), which contains no breach-notification article. However, a 2025/2026 AML compliance guide (ANQA) asserts regulated entities must notify the CDP and financial supervisors of material breaches 'without undue delay,' and a generic legal content site cites a 72-hour window, neither citing a specific statutory provision. Given the direct legal-text analysis contradicts the more generic recent guidance, and no primary regulation could be fetched to resolve this, the score is left at 0/Unknown and flagged for human review rather than guessed.
revised_comments: Evidence on Senegal's payment data breach notification requirements is mixed. Legal analysis of the founding Data Protection Act (Law No. 2008-12 of 25 January 2008), which does not contain an explicit breach-notification article, indicates there is no general statutory obligation to notify the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles (CDP) or affected individuals of a data breach. More recent compliance guidance for regulated financial entities describes an expectation to notify the CDP and financial supervisors of material breaches without undue delay, though without citing the specific legal basis for this obligation.

Fetched and read the full text of Law No. 2008-12 (via WIPO Lex) and the DLA Piper Data Protection Laws of the World summary. The Act is a general data protection law covering all collection, processing, storage and transmission of personal data by public and private bodies, which would extend to payment transaction data as a subset of personal data, but it contains no provisions specific to payment or financial data. revised_comments: Senegal has a comprehensive general data protection law, Act No. 2008-12 of 25 January 2008 Concerning Personal Data Protection, implemented by Decree No. 2008-721 of 30 June 2008 and enforced by the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles (CDP). The Act covers all collection, processing, transmission, storage and use of personal data by individuals, the state, local authorities and public or private bodies, which extends by definition to payment transaction data, although the Act contains no provisions specific to payment or financial transaction data.

revised_comments: No single, current, authoritative percentage for the share of government-to-person (G2P) disbursements (salaries, pensions, social transfers) made digitally in Senegal is available. A 2018 Better Than Cash Alliance diagnostic found government payments to businesses and authorities (administrative expenditure) were nearly 100% digitised, while explicitly noting social programmes lagged behind. Since 2022, the Senegalese Agency for Universal Health Coverage (SEN-CSU) has digitised enrolment and premium payments for its health cover scheme, covering over 50% of the population, illustrating sector-specific progress, though no comprehensive G2P digitisation percentage across all programmes has been published.
